topic.title: MCP-1 From Aging Dermal Adipose Tissue Impairs Hair Follicle Cycling via Macrophage Recruitment: Implications for Age-Related Alopecia
topic.abstract: Aging leads to significant hair changes, including alopecia and graying, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Emerging evidence highlights the role of the extracellular microenvironment, particularly dermal white adipose tissue (dWAT), in regulating hair regeneration and pigmentation. Previous studies showed that young murine dWAT improves age-related hair phenotypes via follistatin upregulation. This study investigates key molecular mechanisms in dWAT governing hair aging, aiming to inform targeted therapies for age-related hair disorders. Using in vivo murine models, protein arrays, FACS, immunofluorescence, and transcriptomics, we identified monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) as a critical factor secreted by aged dWAT. MCP-1 recruits macrophages to perifollicular regions. Depleting skin macrophages in aged mice shifted hair follicles from telogen to anagen and upregulated melanocyte-lineage proteins, including DCT, Tyrosinase-related protein 1 (TYRP1), and Pmel17. Transcriptomic analysis revealed macrophage absence activated signaling pathways essential for hair growth and melanogenesis, upregulating hair follicle development genes. Conversely, M0 and M2 macrophages were associated with earlier anagen entry, whereas M1 macrophages delayed anagen transition. These findings identify dWAT as a pivotal regulator of age-associated hair changes, in which MCP-1-mediated macrophage accumulation is critically involved.
